# Mayneord-like tumour growth inhibition and IC50 coverage for stasis

Huber and Mistry (2024) link the empirical in-vitro to in-vivo correlation
(IVIVC) used in oncology drug discovery -- tumour growth inhibition (TGI)
plotted against the ratio of the unbound average plasma concentration to the
unbound in-vitro IC50 -- to a semi-mechanistic tumour growth model. The tumour
radius `R` grows linearly at a xenograft-specific rate `g` (a Mayneord-like
model of a proliferating rim around a necrotic core) and is reduced at a
xenograft-specific maximal rate `d` scaled by the compound's in-vitro Hill
function of the unbound plasma concentration `C(t)`:

```
dR/dt = g - d * C(t)^hill / (C(t)^hill + IC50^hill)       (Eq. 8, 19, 30)
V     = 4/3 * pi * R^3                                      (Eq. 1)
```

The paper derives closed-form stasis conditions for a steady-state
mono-exponential PK profile, summarised by the *model efficacy factor*
`MEF(PTR, g/d, hill)` -- the IC50 coverage of the unbound average
concentration that just halts tumour growth (Eq. 28 and 33) -- and shows that
for `hill = 1` the coverage depends far more on the xenograft's `g/d` ratio
than on the compound's peak-trough ratio (PTR).

The only parameter values fitted to data come from Appendix A, where the
authors re-analysed the published PI3K-pathway inhibitor xenograft studies of
Diegmiller et al. (2022) and obtained `g` and `d` for two breast-cancer
cell-line xenografts. Each xenograft is a separate model file:

| Model file | Xenograft | g (mm/day) | d (mm/day) | g/d | Default IC50 (taselisib, umol/L) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Huber_2024_tgi_hcc1954_mouse` | HCC1954 | 0.09 | 0.16 | 0.56 | 0.106 |
| `Huber_2024_tgi_kpl4_mouse`    | KPL-4   | 0.20 | 0.30 | 0.67 | 0.0622 |

The models are PD-only: the unbound plasma concentration is supplied as the
time-varying covariate `CEFFECT`, in the same unit as `IC50`. The IC50 is a
property of the compound in the cell line; override `lic50` to simulate
another compound.

## Population

The models describe mouse xenografts of the human breast-cancer cell lines
HCC1954 and KPL-4. The data are the dose-group summaries tabulated in the
paper's Appendix A supplementary CSV: 36 HCC1954 dose groups (GDC-0032
taselisib, GDC-0068 ipatasertib, GDC-0077 inavolisib, GDC-0941 pictilisib;
0.39-150 mg/kg; 11 Diegmiller study IDs) and 29 KPL-4 dose groups (alpelisib,
GDC-0032, GDC-0077, GDC-0941; 0.2-150 mg/kg; 9 study IDs). The number of
animals is not reported. The main-text IVIVC (Figure 1) uses Boehringer
Ingelheim's internal MAPK-inhibitor xenograft data (86 experiments, 6
xenografts, 12 compounds), for which no xenograft-level `g` or `d` values are
published, so it contributes no model file.

## Load the models

```{r load-models}
mod_hcc <- readModelDb("Huber_2024_tgi_hcc1954_mouse")
mod_kpl <- readModelDb("Huber_2024_tgi_kpl4_mouse")
mod_hcc
```

## Appendix A: re-analysis of the Diegmiller 2022 xenografts

Huber and Mistry converted each dose group's initial and final tumour volume
to a spherical radius and divided the change by the study duration, giving an
observed net radial growth rate. With the unbound average concentration
`Cavg` of each dose group held constant, the model predicts a constant net
rate `g - d * Cavg / (Cavg + IC50)`. The 65 dose groups below are the
paper's supplementary CSV (Cavg and GI50 in umol/L, rates in mm/day).

Each dose group is simulated for 21 days with `CEFFECT` held at its `Cavg`
and `lic50` set to the compound's GI50; the model's net radial rate is the
change in radius divided by the duration.

```{r appendix-a-sim}
models <- list(HCC1954 = mod_hcc, "KPL-4" = mod_kpl)
t_end <- 21

simulate_group <- function(cell_line, compound) {
  rows <- filter(csv, cell == cell_line, drug == compound)
  ev <- rows |>
    select(id, cavg) |>
    crossing(time = c(0, t_end)) |>
    mutate(evid = 0L, cmt = "tumor_size", CEFFECT = cavg) |>
    select(id, time, evid, cmt, CEFFECT) |>
    arrange(id, time)
  rxSolve(
    models[[cell_line]], ev,
    params = c(lic50 = log(rows$gi50[1])),
    returnType = "data.frame"
  ) |>
    group_by(id) |>
    summarise(sim_net = (last(tumor_size) - first(tumor_size)) / t_end, .groups = "drop")
}

net <- csv |>
  distinct(cell, drug) |>
  rowwise() |>
  reframe(simulate_group(cell, drug)) |>
  select(id, sim_net) |>
  right_join(csv, by = "id")

# Known-answer check: the model reproduces the authors' predicted net rate of
# every dose group (same equation, deterministic; differences are rounding of
# the CSV to nine significant figures).
stopifnot(max(abs(net$sim_net - net$pub_pred_net)) < 1e-6)
max(abs(net$sim_net - net$pub_pred_net))
```

```{r fig8, fig.cap = "Replicates Figure 8 of Huber 2024: model-predicted versus observed net radial growth rates for the Diegmiller 2022 xenograft studies. Line of identity shown."}
ggplot(net, aes(obs_net, sim_net, shape = drug, colour = factor(dose))) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~cell) +
  labs(
    x = "Observed net rate (mm/day)", y = "Predicted net rate (mm/day)",
    shape = "Compound", colour = "Dose (mg/kg)"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

The fit is markedly better in HCC1954 than in KPL-4, where alpelisib and
GDC-0941 dose groups scatter widely -- as in the published figure.

```{r fit-summary}
net |>
  group_by(cell) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    `Median |obs - pred| (mm/day)` = median(abs(obs_net - sim_net)),
    `Correlation obs vs pred` = cor(obs_net, sim_net)
  ) |>
  rename("Cell line" = cell) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

## Tumour volume time course and TGI

A 21-day simulation of taselisib in HCC1954 at three of the published dose
groups' average unbound concentrations, with a vehicle control. TGI follows
Eq. 9 from the volume change over the treatment period.

```{r tumour-course}
tas <- csv |>
  filter(cell == "HCC1954", drug == "GDC-0032", study == 8, dose %in% c(1.56, 6.25, 12.5)) |>
  select(dose, cavg) |>
  bind_rows(tibble(dose = 0, cavg = 0)) |>
  mutate(id = row_number())

ev_tc <- tas |>
  crossing(time = seq(0, t_end, by = 0.5)) |>
  mutate(evid = 0L, cmt = "tumor_size", CEFFECT = cavg) |>
  select(id, time, evid, cmt, CEFFECT)

tc <- rxSolve(mod_hcc, ev_tc, returnType = "data.frame") |>
  left_join(select(tas, id, dose), by = "id")

ggplot(tc, aes(time, tumor_vol, colour = factor(dose))) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Time (day)", y = "Tumour volume (mm^3)", colour = "Taselisib (mg/kg)") +
  theme_bw()

dv <- tc |>
  group_by(dose) |>
  summarise(dV = last(tumor_vol) - first(tumor_vol), .groups = "drop")
tgi <- dv |>
  mutate(TGI = 100 * (1 - dV / dV[dose == 0])) |>
  filter(dose > 0)
knitr::kable(tgi |> rename("Dose (mg/kg)" = dose, "Volume change (mm^3)" = dV, "TGI (%)" = TGI), digits = c(2, 1, 1))

# TGI rises with dose and exceeds 100% (regression) once d * f(Cavg) > g.
stopifnot(all(diff(tgi$TGI) > 0), tail(tgi$TGI, 1) > 100)
```

## Stasis analysis with a steady-state PK profile

Sections 3.3-3.5 assume a steady-state, mono-exponential unbound profile
falling from `cmax` to `ctrough` over each dosing interval `tau` (Eq. 22).
Tumour stasis over the interval requires the IC50 coverage of the average
concentration to equal the model efficacy factor (Eq. 28 and 33):

```
MEF(PTR, g/d, hill) = (PTR - 1)/ln(PTR) * [(PTR^(hill*g/d) - 1) / (PTR^hill - PTR^(hill*g/d))]^(1/hill)
```

```{r mef-functions}
mef <- function(ptr, gd, hill = 1) {
  (ptr - 1) / log(ptr) * ((ptr^(hill * gd) - 1) / (ptr^hill - ptr^(hill * gd)))^(1 / hill)
}
ctrough_cov <- function(ptr, gd) (ptr^gd - 1) / (ptr - ptr^gd) # Eq. 26
cmax_cov <- function(ptr, gd) ptr * ctrough_cov(ptr, gd) # Eq. 26
```

The closed form is first checked against the authors' own spreadsheet
(supplementary XLSX, sheet 'Sheet2', which tabulates MEF for `hill = 1`):

```{r mef-xlsx}
xlsx <- tribble(
  ~gd, ~ptr, ~mef_pub,
  0.3, 3, 0.4415322386239014, 0.3, 30, 0.55563010705857541, 0.3, 100, 0.66742900838381913, 0.3, 1000, 1.0121779420104093,
  0.5, 3, 1.0510537250399223, 0.5, 30, 1.5567021831085632, 0.5, 100, 2.149757685421096, 0.5, 1000, 4.5732879277299885,
  0.7, 3, 2.5020006157722401, 0.7, 30, 4.3613937691815803, 0.7, 100, 6.9242691701667871, 0.7, 1000, 20.663325687950774
) |>
  mutate(mef_eq28 = mef(ptr, gd))
stopifnot(max(abs(xlsx$mef_eq28 / xlsx$mef_pub - 1)) < 1e-10)
knitr::kable(xlsx |> rename("g/d" = gd, "PTR" = ptr, "MEF (XLSX)" = mef_pub, "MEF (Eq. 28)" = mef_eq28), digits = 4)
```

The ODE is then driven by the steady-state profile at exactly the stasis
average concentration `Cavg = MEF * IC50`. If Eq. 28 / 33 are the correct
integrals of the model, the radius returns to its starting value at the end of
every dosing interval. The profile is supplied on a dense grid with linear
interpolation; `g/d` is varied through `lemax` (`d = g / (g/d)`).

```{r stasis-ode}
tau <- 1 # day
grid <- seq(0, 2 * tau, by = tau / 2000)
theta_hcc <- rxode2::rxode2(mod_hcc)$theta
g_hcc <- exp(theta_hcc[["lp"]])
ic50_hcc <- exp(theta_hcc[["lic50"]])

stasis_cases <- crossing(gd = c(0.3, 0.4, 0.5, 0.6, 0.7), ptr = c(3, 10, 30, 100, 300, 1000), hill = c(1, 2)) |>
  mutate(
    cavg = mef(ptr, gd, hill) * ic50_hcc,
    # c_average = (cmax - ctrough) / ln(PTR) with ctrough = cmax / PTR
    cmax = cavg * log(ptr) / (1 - 1 / ptr)
  )

solve_stasis <- function(gd, hill, cases) {
  ev <- cases |>
    mutate(id = row_number()) |>
    crossing(time = grid) |>
    mutate(
      evid = 0L, cmt = "tumor_size",
      CEFFECT = cmax * exp(-log(ptr) / tau * (time %% tau))
    ) |>
    select(id, time, evid, cmt, CEFFECT)
  rxSolve(
    mod_hcc, ev,
    params = c(lemax = log(g_hcc / gd), hill = hill),
    covsInterpolation = "linear", atol = 1e-10, rtol = 1e-10,
    returnType = "data.frame"
  ) |>
    group_by(id) |>
    summarise(dR = last(tumor_size) - first(tumor_size), .groups = "drop") |>
    mutate(ptr = cases$ptr[id])
}

stasis <- stasis_cases |>
  group_by(gd, hill) |>
  group_modify(~ solve_stasis(.y$gd, .y$hill, .x)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  # Radius change over two intervals relative to untreated growth g * 2 * tau
  mutate(rel_dR = dR / (g_hcc * 2 * tau))

# Residual is the linear interpolation across the sawtooth's dose-time jump,
# well under 1% of untreated growth.
stopifnot(max(abs(stasis$rel_dR)) < 0.01)
stasis |>
  group_by(hill) |>
  summarise(`max |dR| / (g * T)` = max(abs(rel_dR))) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 5)
```

Driving the model at half and at twice the stasis concentration confirms the
condition is a threshold: the tumour grows below it and regresses above it.

```{r stasis-threshold}
thr <- crossing(gd = 0.5, ptr = 100, hill = 1, scale = c(0.5, 1, 2)) |>
  mutate(cavg = scale * mef(ptr, gd, hill) * ic50_hcc, cmax = cavg * log(ptr) / (1 - 1 / ptr))
thr_res <- solve_stasis(0.5, 1, thr) |> mutate(scale = thr$scale)
stopifnot(thr_res$dR[1] > 0.01, thr_res$dR[3] < -0.01)
knitr::kable(thr_res |> select("Multiple of stasis Cavg" = scale, "Radius change over 2 days (mm)" = dR), digits = 4)
```

### Figure 3: coverage required for stasis by cmax, c_average and ctrough

```{r fig3, fig.cap = "Replicates Figure 3 of Huber 2024 (hill = 1). Lines: Eq. 26; points: steady-state ODE solutions at the stasis c_average. Drawn at g/d = 0.5, the ratio that reproduces the published curves (see Assumptions)."}
fig3 <- tibble(ptr = seq(1.05, 100, length.out = 300)) |>
  mutate(
    c_max = cmax_cov(ptr, 0.5),
    c_average = mef(ptr, 0.5),
    c_trough = ctrough_cov(ptr, 0.5)
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(-ptr, names_to = "metric", values_to = "coverage")
fig3_ode <- stasis |>
  filter(gd == 0.5, hill == 1, ptr <= 100) |>
  mutate(coverage = mef(ptr, gd))
ggplot(fig3, aes(ptr, coverage, linetype = metric)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(data = fig3_ode, aes(ptr, coverage), inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "Peak-trough ratio", y = "In-vitro IC50 coverage for stasis", linetype = NULL) +
  theme_bw()
```

### Figure 4: MEF versus the xenograft g/d ratio

```{r fig4, fig.cap = "Replicates Figure 4 of Huber 2024 (hill = 1). Dashed line: MEF = 2."}
fig4 <- crossing(gd = seq(0.01, 0.9, by = 0.01), ptr = c(3, 10, 30, 50, 100, 300, 500)) |>
  mutate(MEF = mef(ptr, gd))
ggplot(fig4, aes(gd, MEF, colour = factor(ptr))) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 2, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "growth / decay (g/d) ratio of xenograft", colour = "PTR") +
  theme_bw()
```

The paper states that for `g/d` between 0.3 and 0.7 and PTR between 40 and
150, the coverage ranges from about half to about ten-fold IC50:

```{r fig4-range}
range(mef(c(40, 150), c(0.3, 0.7)))
```

### Figure 5: MEF versus PTR for Hill coefficients above 1

```{r fig5, fig.cap = "Replicates Figure 5 of Huber 2024 (Eq. 33, g/d = 0.5). Points: steady-state ODE solutions for hill = 2 at g/d = 0.5."}
fig5 <- crossing(ptr = seq(1.05, 100, length.out = 300), hill = seq(1, 1.9, by = 0.1)) |>
  mutate(MEF = mef(ptr, 0.5, hill))
fig5_ode <- stasis |>
  filter(gd == 0.5, hill == 2, ptr <= 100) |>
  mutate(MEF = mef(ptr, gd, hill))
ggplot(fig5, aes(ptr, MEF, group = hill, colour = hill)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(data = fig5_ode, aes(ptr, MEF), inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "Peak-trough ratio", y = "MEF (g/d, PTR, hill)", colour = "Hill") +
  theme_bw()
```

## Empirical IVIVC and the stasis dose

The empirical logistic fit of the internal data set (Eq. 10; PDinflex = 0.25,
hillexp = 0.89, TGImax = 125, TGImin = 0) gives the coverage of the unbound
average concentration needed for TGI = 100% (Eq. 13 and 16):

```{r ivivc}
pd_inflex <- 0.25
hill_exp <- 0.89
tgi_max <- 125
tgi_min <- 0
coverage_stasis <- pd_inflex * ((tgi_max - tgi_min) / 100 - 1)^(-1 / hill_exp)
c(coverage_cavg = coverage_stasis, coverage_auc_tau24h = 24 * coverage_stasis)
```

The paper prints 1.24 and 29.8 (Eq. 15-16); the rounded fit parameters give
1.19 and 28.5, a 4% difference consistent with rounding of `hillexp` (a
value of 0.86 reproduces 1.25).

## PKNCA

PKNCA is not applicable: the models carry no pharmacokinetics (the unbound
concentration is an input covariate) and the output is a tumour radius.
Validation instead rests on the known-answer checks above -- the Appendix A
net rates, the closed-form stasis conditions and the authors' MEF spreadsheet.

# Assumptions and deviations

- **Concentration driver.** The unbound plasma concentration enters as
  `CEFFECT`. The paper assumes the free-plasma-drug hypothesis with no delay
  between unbound plasma and the tumour, so the unbound plasma concentration
  is the effect-site concentration.
- **Units.** The Appendix A supplementary CSV does not label the
  concentration unit of `Cavg` and `GI50`. The models declare umol/L, the
  unit in which Diegmiller et al. (2022) report these in-vitro potencies
  (median taselisib IC50 0.089 uM across PIK3CA-mutant lines, against 0.106
  for HCC1954 here). Only the ratio `CEFFECT / IC50` enters the model, so any
  unit works as long as both use it.
- **Initial radius.** No initial radius is reported for the Diegmiller
  xenografts. Supplement 1 (section 1) states 'R0 ~ 3 cm' for the authors'
  own studies alongside g ~ 0.01 mm/h; a 3 cm radius would be a 113 cm^3
  tumour, so the maintainers read it as 3 mm (113 mm^3, a typical xenograft
  starting volume) and fixed `lrbase` at log(3). R0 does not affect the
  radial growth or decay rates; override it for a given experiment.
- **Hill coefficient.** Fixed at 1, as in the Appendix A re-analysis (the
  CSV's predicted net rates are reproduced exactly with hill = 1). The
  general form (Eq. 7, 30) is retained so `hill` can be overridden.
- **Constant Cavg in Appendix A.** The authors drove the re-analysis with
  each dose group's average concentration rather than a time-varying
  profile. Because the Hill function is concave, a constant concentration
  has more effect than a fluctuating profile with the same average (the
  stasis analysis above quantifies this through the MEF), so `d` estimated
  this way is specific to the constant-input approximation. The replicate
  uses the constant input because the published predictions do.
- **Figure 3 and 5 g/d.** The Figure 3 caption and Section 3.4 give
  g/d = 0.4, but the published curves (c_average coverage of about 2.15 and
  c_max coverage of 10 at PTR = 100) are reproduced only at g/d = 0.5, which
  is what the replicates use.
- **No variability.** The paper reports no between-animal variability or
  residual error, so the models are deterministic.
- **Internal MAPK-inhibitor data.** The Boehringer Ingelheim IVIVC data set
  (Figure 1, 6) reports only a typical g/d of about 0.4 (range 0.3-0.7) and
  no xenograft-level parameter values, so it is not encoded as a model; its
  empirical logistic fit is evaluated above.
- **Errata.** No correction notice for Huber and Mistry (2024) was found on
  Europe PMC as of 2026-10-29.
